title_en: Rare Heron Returns to Thornwick Marshes
title_ru: Редкая цапля вернулась на болота Торнвика
description_ru: Вымышленная новость о возвращении редкой цапли на восстановленные болота Торнвика и о том, чего это стоило местным жителям и волонтёрам.
text:
THORNWICK - A pair of purple herons, one of the rarest breeding birds in Britain, have nested on the Thornwick Marshes for the first time in more than a century, delighting conservationists and drawing a stream of binocular-wielding visitors to a corner of the countryside that was, until recently, regarded as an expensive failure.

The nest, an untidy platform of reeds roughly the size of a bicycle wheel, was discovered on 9 May by a volunteer warden, Philomena Ashby, who was counting reed warblers at dawn. "I saw a long, rusty-coloured neck rising out of the reeds and thought I had imagined it," she said. "Then it turned its head and I saw the stripes. I sat down in the mud and could not speak for several minutes. I think I may have wept a little."

Purple herons are slimmer and more secretive than their grey cousins, with chestnut plumage, dark stripes along the neck and a dagger-like bill. They breed in dense reedbeds across southern Europe and the Netherlands, and only occasional wanderers reach Britain, most of them young birds blown off course in spring. A confirmed breeding attempt is almost unheard of; the last recorded nest was in a Norfolk marsh in the early twentieth century, before the drainage of the fens destroyed most of the habitat.

Thornwick itself owes its transformation to a stubborn and, at times, unpopular project. Until the 1990s the marshes were drained farmland, where a single farmer grew wheat on soil that sank a little further each year as the peat dried and blew away. When the owner retired, a conservation charity bought the land for a sum that astonished the neighbours, and set about reversing a century of drainage. Pumps were switched off, channels were blocked and the fields were allowed to flood.

The early years were difficult. Local farmers complained that the water was spilling onto their land, and the charity was accused by one newspaper of "turning good fields into a swamp". A neighbouring landowner, Cuthbert Pryce, who grazes cattle beside the reserve, remembers the period with a rueful smile. "I told them they were mad," he said. "I thought the whole thing would be a mess of mosquitoes and mud. I had to be honest, and I was wrong. The place has more birdsong in an hour than my farm has in a month."

The recovery took patience. Reeds took nearly ten years to form a dense bed, and the first breeding success was a pair of bitterns, a notoriously shy relative of the heron, in 2009. Since then the reserve has been colonised by marsh harriers, otters and spoonbills, and the water voles that had vanished from the area have returned in healthy numbers. The charity's director, Dr Anselm Rooke, describes the herons as the "crowning moment" of a thirty-year experiment, but he is careful not to overstate its significance. "A single nest is a promise, not a guarantee," he said. "The birds still have to raise their chicks, and there are many things that can go wrong: a late frost, a fox, a bad flood. We will not celebrate until they fledge."

To reduce the risks, the reserve has imposed strict restrictions around the nest. The reedbed has been closed to the public, a fence has been installed to deter foxes and a team of volunteers is keeping watch in shifts from a hide half a kilometre away. The location is not marked on any map, and visitors are being asked not to publish photographs that might reveal it. Staff have been dismayed by reports that a handful of photographers had tried to approach the nest, and the charity has warned that anyone disturbing a rare breeding bird could face prosecution.

The excitement has not been confined to birdwatchers. The village of Thornwick, whose population is fewer than six hundred, has experienced a modest boom. The Wheatsheaf, its only public house, has introduced a "heron breakfast" that sells out by nine, and the owner of the nearby bed-and-breakfast says that every room has been booked until the end of July. "I have lived here for fifty years," said the publican, Gwendoline Marsh, "and I have never seen the car park full on a Tuesday. If the birds can bring this many people, they are welcome to stay as long as they like."

Scientists say that the arrival is likely to be linked to the changing climate. Warmer winters in southern Europe have encouraged populations of purple herons to expand northwards, and the Thornwick reedbed, with its abundant fish and amphibians, offers an ideal landing place. Dr Rooke warned that the news should not be allowed to obscure the broader picture: more than half of Britain's wetlands have been lost since the Roman period, and many species that depend on them are still declining.

Walkers on the nearby footpath, many of them carrying flasks and folding stools, have formed a cheerful, whispering community of their own. For the volunteers who watch the nest, the prospect of failure is a daily worry. On Sunday, the female was seen standing on the platform with her wings half open, shading what the wardens believe to be three eggs from the heat of the sun. If all goes well, they should hatch in about three weeks. Philomena Ashby has volunteered for the dawn shift every morning until then. "I have no intention of missing it," she said, and went back to her notebook.

questions.question: What rare event happened at Thornwick Marshes?
questions.answer: Purple herons nested there for the first time in over a century.

questions.question: How was the land changed before the birds came?
questions.answer: Drained farmland was flooded by switching off pumps and blocking channels.

questions.question: What precautions protect the nest?
questions.answer: The reedbed is closed, there is a fence, and volunteers keep watch.

questions.question: How has the village benefited?
questions.answer: Visitors fill the pub, car park and bed-and-breakfast rooms.
